source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: The founding LLM debate paper. Several ChatGPT agents see each other's answers and revise over rounds. Debate beat single agent, reflection and majority vote on all tasks. The authors note agents converge on one shared answer after a few rounds.
numbers: 3 agents, 2 rounds. Arithmetic 67.0 single, 69.0 majority, 81.8 debate. GSM8K 77.0 single, 81.0 majority, 85.0 debate. Chess pawn score 91.4 single, 102.2 majority, 122.9 debate.
quote: Empirically, however, we find that language models are able to converge on a single shared answer
limits: Early ChatGPT only. Later work with matched cost and stronger baselines does not reproduce the margin over voting (see c06, c07, c09). Convergence is reported as a feature, not tested as a risk.
agent_relevance: Source of the consensus-seeking loop that G9 argues against. The gain of 4 to 13 points over majority here is the claim later papers shrink.

source: Liang et al. (2023/2024) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Self-reflection suffers Degeneration-of-Thought: once a model is confident it does not change even when wrong. Two debaters told to 'tit for tat' plus a judge fix this. Forcing disagreement on every point was not best.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive AR accuracy: GPT-3.5 26.0, CoT 28.0, self-consistency 29.5, self-reflect 27.5, MAD 37.0, GPT-4 51.0. Translation human score (lexical) 3.14 for GPT-4 Turbo base vs 3.78 with MAD. Disagreement level 0.988 (must disagree on every point) was not the best setting.
quote: asking the debaters to 'tit for tat' (i.e., higher disagreement) is necessary for MAD to achieve good performance
limits: Disagreement is an imposed role. The judge shows a preference bias between debaters. Long debates strain context. Strong debaters with a weak judge works better than the reverse.
agent_relevance: Some imposed disagreement beats agreement-seeking, but there is a sweet spot. Do not push to maximal dissent.

source: Sharma et al. (2023/2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Five AI assistants wrongly give in when a user challenges a correct answer. Human preference data and preference models favour agreeable answers over truthful ones, so training pushes toward agreement.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits a mistake on 98% of questions where it had no mistake (are-you-sure test). Holds even when the model stated high confidence.
quote: models tend to admit mistakes even when they didn't make a mistake
limits: Tests user-to-model pressure, not peer-model pressure. Later work (c15) finds base models also yield, so RLHF is not the only cause.
agent_relevance: Baseline reason an LLM panel drifts to premature agreement. A scaffold cannot rely on the model to hold a correct view under pushback.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (with demonstrations) matches the best multi-agent discussion across reasoning tasks. Discussion helps mainly when no demonstration is given. The most common discussion error is wrong answer propagation: an agent drops a correct view and joins an incorrect consensus.
numbers: Compared ReConcile, CMD (group discussion), Debate, MAD against single agent on FOLIO-wiki, ECQA, GSM8K and others. Debate and CMD got worse on ECQA when demonstrations were added.
quote: This is the most common mistake the multi-agent discussion can make, even when most of their initial answers are correct
limits: Exact percentage gaps not extracted from the tables. Prompt design drives much of the result.
agent_relevance: Names two failure types to guard against: judge mistake on ties, and wrong answer propagation. Supports spending effort on one strong prompt first.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs
finding: Benchmarked debate methods (Society of Mind, Multi-Persona, ChatEval, Ensemble Refinement) against self-consistency and Medprompt. Debate did not reliably win and is hyperparameter sensitive. Tuning the prompted agreement level helped a lot.
numbers: On a 376-question USMLE subset, raising prompted agreement intensity (about 90% used on full MedQA) lifted Multi-Persona by about 15 points and Society of Mind by about 5; ChatEval barely moved. Multi-Persona went from worst to best protocol. On non-medical sets single agents beat all but Multi-Persona and self-consistency.
limits: Agreement level is set by prompt; the induced consensus differs by system. Results rest on a handful of datasets.
agent_relevance: Agreement strength is a dial, and wrong settings cost accuracy. Do not assume fixed always-agree or always-disagree.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate - We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
finding: Five MAD methods on 9 benchmarks and 4 models mostly fail to beat plain chain of thought, and lose more clearly to self-consistency, while using more compute. Mixing different base models (Heter-MAD) gave gains for every method tried.
numbers: 36 configurations (4 models x 9 datasets), ANOVA at 0.05. SoM, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15% of cases; Multi-Persona no significant gain. GPT-4o-mini: SoM below CoT on all 9 sets; ChatEval and AgentVerse above CoT on 1 of 9. Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU: only AgentVerse above CoT (+0.85); others at least 3.60 below.
limits: Position paper with a large evaluation. MAD does beat direct answering without CoT.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G9. Heterogeneous models, not more talk, is where the gain is.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs?
finding: Splits debate into majority voting and talking. Voting alone gives most of the gain. Proof: debate induces a martingale over belief, so talk alone does not raise expected correctness.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B, 5 agents, 7 benchmarks, average accuracy: single 0.7205, decentralized MAD (T=2) 0.7377, (T=5) 0.7050, sparse (T=2) 0.7330, centralized (T=2) 0.6551, majority vote 0.7691. Llama3.1-8B: single 0.6203, decentralized T=2 0.6929, centralized T=5 0.5670, majority vote 0.7242.
quote: Majority Voting alone accounts for most of the performance gains typically attributed to MAD
limits: Theory assumes a Dirichlet-multinomial belief model. Mean accuracy across rounds stays flat. A central aggregator agent was clearly worst.
agent_relevance: Strongest formal and empirical backing for G9: more rounds add no accuracy, and a summariser agent can lower it by 8 to 15 points.

source: Kaesberg et al. (2025) Voting or Consensus? Decision-Making in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Seven decision rules (4 voting, 3 consensus) with only the rule changed. Voting is better for reasoning, consensus for knowledge. More discussion rounds before voting lower accuracy; more agents raise it.
numbers: Voting beat consensus by 13.2% on reasoning; consensus beat voting by 2.8% on knowledge tasks. Consensus needed 1.42 rounds, voting 3.38. Approval voting failed to reach a decision in 59% of cases because agents approve everything. Unanimity did best on unanswerable SQuAD 2.0 items. All-Agents Drafting +3.3%, Collective Improvement +7.4%. Llama 3 8B main, 70B in appendix.
limits: Sampled subsets, three runs. Agents are role personas.
agent_relevance: Quick unanimity is not better on reasoning. Independent drafts before any talk (AAD) is a cheap fix.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate lowers accuracy versus majority vote of the initial answers in many mixes of GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B. Even groups with a strong majority lose. Accuracy often falls across rounds. Correct to incorrect flips outnumber incorrect to correct flips.
numbers: 100 questions x 5 seeds. Diverse group (one of each model): MMLU 40.0 to 28.0 (-12.0), CSQA 53.4 to 46.8, GSM8K 61.0 to 64.8. Another mix MMLU 33.6 to 24.4 (-9.2). On CommonsenseQA debate lowered accuracy in every reported group. Single agent: GPT-4o-mini 74.8/82.6/93.2 (CSQA/MMLU/GSM8K), Mistral 41.6/34.0/34.2.
quote: models frequently shift from correct to incorrect answers in response to peer reasoning, favoring agreement over challenging flawed reasoning
limits: Small samples, small models, three tasks. GSM8K sometimes improves (up to +4.4).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for premature agreement in LLM panels: weak members drag strong members down.

source: Wynn et al. (2025) flip rate versus number of agreeing peers
finding: An agent's chance of flipping from right to wrong is highest when it stands alone (no peer agrees) and falls as more peers agree. This is the Asch conformity pattern in models. Resistance is lower in round 2 than in round 1.
numbers: Measured per model and dataset in Figure 4. On GSM8K, GPT and Mistral flip far less than Llama. No exact table values extracted.
limits: Figure-based; variation across datasets and models is large.
agent_relevance: A lone correct dissenter in a panel will tend to be overruled, so dissent must be structurally protected.

source: Wynn et al. (2025) correctness-payoff prompt as a sycophancy fix
finding: Telling agents they are paid for a correct final answer (an incentive idea from political science) did not reduce harmful flips and often raised them.
numbers: Tested on GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B over CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K, with 0, 1 or 2 agreeing peers.
limits: One prompt wording only. Authors say no single cause explains the failure.
agent_relevance: A 'be accurate' instruction is not a defence against consensus drift. Matches the schema stance that reasoning text is not evidence.

source: Yao et al. (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Defines disagreement collapse rate (DCR): cases where at least one agent held the right answer at the start but the group did not keep it. Highly sycophantic debaters do worst. A judge cuts collapse.
numbers: Homogeneous Llama3.3-70B DCR up to 86.36% (2-agent CommonsenseQA), no gain over single agent. Centralized judge: Qwen-Qwen accuracy 83.62 to 86.65 with DCR 81.71 to 41.27; Qwen-Llama 81.00 to 86.49 with DCR 80.41 to 35.51. 45 persona mixes homogeneous: accuracy 81.98 to 83.87, lowest when both 'peacemaker'. 81 mixes heterogeneous: 78.95 to 82.06, best when both 'troublemaker'.
quote: sycophancy ... can collapse debates into premature consensus
limits: Two datasets, two model families. Persona control gains are small in homogeneous groups. Three-agent debates have lower DCR than two-agent.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable quantity our agent can log: did anyone hold the right answer and then lose it?

source: Controlled study of LLM debate on Knight-Knave-Spy puzzles (2025) Can LLM Agents Really Debate?
finding: With exact ground truth, debate success is set by the strongest reasoner and by diversity. Majority pressure suppresses independent correction; weak teams converge early on wrong or persuasive but unsound reasoning.
numbers: Debate raised instance accuracy by 52% (size-4 puzzles) and 32% (size-8). An agent in a correct majority stays correct above 97%. In a wrong majority, correction is 34.4% (gemini-2.5-flash) and 30.0% (gpt-5-mini); gemini-2.5-flash-lite only 3.6%. Confidence visibility, order and depth gave negligible effect for weak teams.
limits: One puzzle family. Gains are relative to the initial round, not to a voting baseline.
agent_relevance: Debate helps when at least one strong, receptive reasoner is present. Rely on checkable strong reasoning, not headcount.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes from 1600+ annotated traces across 7 frameworks. Premature termination, weak verification and ignoring other agents' input are among them. Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across the frameworks.
numbers: Premature termination about 6.2%, no or incomplete verification about 8.2%, incorrect verification about 9.1%, ignored other agent's input about 1.9% (figure percentages read from garbled text, may be misaligned). MAST-guided intervention gave +9.4% task success in a case study.
limits: Percent-to-label mapping from the PDF figure is uncertain; treat as approximate.
agent_relevance: Premature stopping and weak verification are common agent-loop faults. Supports an independent final check state.

source: Anonymous authors (2026) Not Just RLHF: Why Alignment Alone Won't Fix Multi-Agent Sycophancy
finding: Correct to incorrect flips under peer pressure (called yield) also occur in pretrained base models, at higher average yield than Instruct. So RLHF does not cause it. Patching places the fault in mid layers (L14 to L18) through attention.
numbers: Yield 44 to 98% of questions a model would otherwise get right when peers disagree or consensus is asserted. Patching above the window restores 96% of the clean-to-pressured gap. Message framing x consensus strength gives a 47.5 point yield gap at majority consensus (user-role framing needs unanimity; assistant or tool role flips at majority). Jury sizes N=4,5,6.
quote: Pressure suppresses clean-reasoning features rather than activating a new sycophancy circuit
limits: Mechanism work mainly on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; behaviour test on four model families. Preprint v3.
agent_relevance: Prompt defences fail off their design surface (best one -65 pp in-design, -14 to -28 pp on other attacks).

source: Not Just RLHF (2026) structured dissent as the defence
finding: A single dissenter who argues the correct answer cuts yield by 54 to 73 points in all three message framings tested. This matches minority influence: one consistent contrarian protects the group.
numbers: Reduction 54 to 73 percentage points across user, assistant and tool framings, versus the strongest prompt defence that works only in its design setting.
quote: A single correctly-arguing dissenter reduces yield by 54-73 percentage points across all framings tested
limits: The dissenter must argue the right answer; a random contrarian was not shown to help. Simulated peer messages, not free debate.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a separate checker or dissent step that argues from evidence.

source: Not All Flips Are Conformity: Decomposing Stance Convergence in Multi-Agent LLM Debate (2026)
finding: Many answer changes happen without any peer, so convergence alone is a poor measure. After a control, 29.3% of stable agent-question pairs adopt a peer answer after seeing peer stances. Adoptions include corrections, new errors and wrong-to-wrong changes.
numbers: Five GPT-4o agents, MMLU-Pro disagreement questions: 37% change with no peer info. Strict conformity 29.30% (CI 27.5 to 31.2, n=960/3277). Flip rates self-reflection 36.98% (MMLU-Pro), 39.24% (GPQA-Diamond); stance-only 46.85%, 46.48%; full reasoning 50.56%, 51.05%. Individual accuracy 42.17% (self-reflection) to 45.87% (full reasoning) but majority vote 77.35% in both, with 57% more tokens. 49.2% of wrong stable targets had no correct peer. Standardised harmful minus beneficial adoption -8.75 pp under stance-only (CI -13.44, -4.27).
quote: convergence is an ambiguous signal of value
limits: Homogeneous single-round GPT-4o main setting; other models in appendix. An answer-agnostic intervention cut both harmful and beneficial adoption with no net gain.
agent_relevance: Never read agreement as evidence of correctness. Log whether a correct option was ever on the table.

source: The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate (2026)
finding: Teams of 10 same-model 7-8B agents, 3 rounds, on GSM-Hard and MMLU-Hard. Debate costs 2.1 to 3.4 times the tokens of isolated self-correction for equal or lower accuracy. Three failure paths: conformity, contextual fragility, consensus collapse.
numbers: Modal adoption up to 85.5%; vulnerability rate (previously correct reasoning destabilised) up to 70.0%; oracle gap (correct answer in pool but plurality discards it) up to 32.3 pp. Up to 28,631 tokens per problem. Conformity high even with 2 peers and rises with initial diversity. Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Ministral-3-8B.
limits: Abstract and first page only; small open models; unstructured roles.
agent_relevance: Cheap isolated self-checks beat naive peer exchange in this model class.

source: Minority Sentinel: When to Overturn Majority Voting in Multi-Agent LLM Debates (2026)
finding: Because LLM errors are correlated, the majority often suppresses a correct minority (named Minority Truth, after Moscovici). A small classifier on debate logs decides when to overturn the vote.
numbers: Three heterogeneous agents, six benchmarks. About one in four divergent cases has the minority right, a roughly 10 pp theoretical recovery margin. Flip precision 81.2% with positive net gain on all six sets and 20 seeds. LLM-as-judge baseline had higher recall but negative net gain.
limits: Abstract and introduction read only. Needs a trained classifier on debate logs.
agent_relevance: Dissent patterns in logs predict when the minority is right. Do not let an LLM judge overturn votes: it lost net accuracy.

source: Group Perspective Matters (DEAR, 2026): Regulating Debate Relationships to Mitigate Blind Conformity
finding: Individual confidence or perplexity scores do not detect blind conformity and can worsen it. DEAR uses group-level consensus and divergence to choose which peers each agent reads, via two RL agents.
numbers: Claims higher accuracy with fewer tokens; exact numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Needs RL training, so not usable in a no-training scaffold.
agent_relevance: Confidence-weighted voting is a weak defence against conformity. Choosing which peers to show is the lever.

source: What Does Multi-Agent Debate Actually Change? (2026)
finding: On 50 GlobalOpinionQA questions, the tone instruction alone changes how much debaters say they agree, but real position change depends on model and interaction. Stated and actual agreement diverge.
numbers: Strong agreement in 70.7 to 96.3% of replies under friendly instructions versus 9.5 to 19.3% under hostile. A text judge rates about one in four replies labelled 'leaning agree' as 'strongly agree'. Two- and three-member committees; same model, same family, mixed.
limits: Opinion questions with no ground truth. Abstract read only.
agent_relevance: One prompt line ('seek common ground') moves reported consensus by about 60 to 77 points: consensus is partly an instruction artifact.

source: Becker et al. (2025/2026) Stay Focused: Problem Drift in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debates drift away from the original problem as turns go on and accuracy falls. DriftJudge detects it; DriftPolicy gives feedback.
numbers: Analysis of 170 debates, ten tasks. Causes: lack of progress 35%, low-quality feedback 26%. Generative tasks drift due to open answer space in 76 to 89% of cases versus 7 to 21% for high-complexity tasks. DriftPolicy fixes 31% of drift cases.
limits: Abstract and intro only (plus search summary). Findings of EACL 2026.
agent_relevance: Long debate has its own cost. Reinforces short loops and re-anchoring to the question.

source: Estornell and Liu (2024) Multi-LLM Debate: Framework, Principals, and Interventions (tyranny of the majority)
finding: Theory and experiments reported to show that when most agents share an answer, minority agents conform and an echo chamber forms regardless of correctness. Known here only through Wynn et al. and Minority Sentinel.
numbers: No numbers read first-hand.
limits: Second-hand description only; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that headcount can lock in a shared error.

source: Kaesberg et al. (2025) rounds and agents ablation
finding: Accuracy falls slightly as discussion rounds before voting rise, and rises as agent count rises. This resembles the self-consistency effect.
numbers: Fixed 3 agents, rounds 1 to 10: slight accuracy drop with more rounds, with a sharp upturn at round 10 noted as an oddity. Fixed 3 rounds, more agents: accuracy up.
limits: Single model family, sampled subsets.
agent_relevance: Prefer width (independent samples) over depth (more discussion).

source: Choi et al. (2025) interventions that bias the belief update toward correction
finding: Because debate is a martingale, only a bias toward correct signals can help. They test designs that nudge updates, including a variant where an agent adopts the previous majority only with 30% probability.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B Table 2 reports modest gains over vanilla debate; a Qwen2.5-32B check on GSM8K and HellaSwag keeps voting as the main source of gain.
limits: Intervention gains are small relative to plain voting. Exact variant numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Make the update step conditional on checkable evidence.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: model mixing in debate
finding: Zhang et al. find heterogeneity helps, Yao et al. find it widens the useful persona range, Wu et al. find the strongest member sets the ceiling. But Wynn et al. find a weak member can hurt a strong one.
numbers: Zhang: Heter-MAD gains in every framework tested. Wynn: adding a weak agent lowers MMLU by up to 12 points. Yao: heterogeneous persona accuracies span 78.95 to 82.06.
limits: Directions differ by whether the weak member is outvoted or persuades.
agent_relevance: A single-model scaffold can vary prompts, but errors correlate more inside one model.
